questiontext.text: The decision tree for the balance-scale coin problem is best described as which kind of tree?

answer.text: A ternary tree (up to three children per node)

feedback.text: Correct — each weighing has three outcomes.

answer.text: A binary tree (two children per node)

feedback.text: Binary would fit a yes/no test; a balance gives three results.
The structure is a rooted decision tree, not a graph.
Each internal node branches on the weighing outcome, so it is a tree.

generalfeedback.text: Because each weighing has three outcomes, the decision tree branches up to three ways at every internal node — a ternary tree.

questiontext.text: To distinguish among N possible cases with a balance scale, the minimum number of weighings is at least which expression?

feedback.text: Correct — k weighings distinguish at most 3^k cases.
That base assumes two outcomes; a balance gives three.
That is far more than needed; the bound is logarithmic base 3.
The relationship is logarithmic, not linear.

generalfeedback.text: Each weighing multiplies the number of distinguishable cases by 3, so k weighings cover 3^k cases and the lower bound is ceil(log base 3 of N).

questiontext.text: In the decision tree, what does the height of the tree represent?

answer.text: The worst-case number of weighings needed

feedback.text: Correct — the longest root-to-leaf path is the worst case.
Height measures path length, not the number of coins.
There is exactly one counterfeit; height is about weighings.
Leaves are the outcomes; height is the longest path to one.

generalfeedback.text: Each level of the tree is one weighing, so the height (longest root-to-leaf path) equals the worst-case number of weighings.

questiontext.text: A single use of a balance scale can distinguish three outcomes, which is why the decision tree is ternary rather than binary.

feedback.text: Correct — left-heavy, balanced, and right-heavy give three outcomes.
The three tilt states make each weighing a three-way branch.

questiontext.text: If the counterfeit among 8 coins is known to be lighter, two weighings are enough to identify it.

feedback.text: Correct — 3^2 = 9 ≥ 8, so two weighings suffice.
With a known-lighter counterfeit there are 8 cases and 3^2 = 9 ≥ 8.
